source.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing

record.file_problem: The supplied post contains an abstract, contribution summary, and comments, but not the full study or its detailed results.
record.tranche_reason: It reports sparse-probing findings about representations in LLMs, extending the study of superposition to a new setting. The supplied text does not give enough detail to establish a direct reproduction of the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: Rows record only findings stated in the supplied abstract and contribution summary. The post does not provide the detailed experiment tables or individual model results. Comments about other work and commenters' interpretations are not treated as study results.
record.test_reason: The study uses k-sparse linear probes on neuron activations in 7 LLMs (70M–6.9B) and reports where features sit in superposition across many polysemantic neurons. That bears directly on V4 (indirect evidence in LLMs). It is a new setting and method, not a toy-model reproduction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that sparse probing locates interpretable neurons, even in superposition, but needs careful follow-up. They find that early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons, with more superposition in the first 25% of layers. Middle layers seemingly have dedicated neurons for higher-level contextual features, though monosemanticity cannot be conclusively established. Sparsity rises with scale on average, with varied feature-specific dynamics.
record.recipe_differences: The study probes internal activations of LLMs using k-sparse linear classifiers; the supplied text does not describe a reproduction of the original toy-model experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary by layer, feature type, and model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: With scale, some features gain dedicated neurons, some split into finer-grained features, and many stay unchanged or appear somewhat randomly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron-level feature representation follows feature-specific scaling dynamics (emergence, splitting, stasis) as LLMs grow.

fits_no_version.finding: Average representation sparsity, measured by probes, increases with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Probe-measured sparsity of feature representations increases with LLM scale.

record.problems: The supplied summary gives qualitative aggregate findings without individual model names, detailed methods, numerical results, uncertainty estimates, or control results. The authors also note that conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed probing experiments are mentioned but not provided in the supplied post text; no additional results can be extracted.

untested.parts: No small toy-network experiments; the sparsity transition and geometry are not tested (toy models are only drawn on for interpretation).
No test that limited capacity or feature importance causes the split between polysemantic and dedicated neurons.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
SAE or dictionary recovery of sparse features is not tested; only the neuron-probing part is.
No test of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Per-model, per-layer probe results (F1 versus k) and the weight-statistics evidence behind the early-layer superposition claim.
missing.locator: Full paper arXiv:2305.01610 (body, figures); not in the post

missing.what: Appendix A discussion relating findings to Toy Models, e.g. why compound-word neurons are superposed while 'French' gets dedicated neurons. Could bear on V2 if it contains evidence beyond interpretation.
missing.locator: Full paper Appendix A (cited in Neel Nanda comment)

record.verdict_notes: Only the abstract and contribution summary were available, so all rows are qualitative aggregates. Comments are not treated as results. The verdicts rest on the summary text, not on the paper's figures.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not report experiments on small toy networks or test the stated sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry.
It reports polysemantic and seemingly dedicated neurons, but does not test whether limited capacity or feature importance causes that division.
It does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through reasons other than capacity pressure.
The post reports sparse probing findings in LLMs, but does not report SAE recovery experiments.
It does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
It does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.operation_detail: Probed for higher-level contextual and linguistic features in neuron activations.
rows.measure: Whether features appear to have dedicated neurons
rows.value: Such features are seemingly encoded by monosemantic neurons.
rows.note: The authors qualify the monosemanticity conclusion as methodologically inconclusive.
rows.check: Dedicated (seemingly monosemantic) neurons for higher-level features in middle layers are the opposite of features spread across many neurons. The state should be 'absent' for V4 in this condition, not 'observed'. The authors say monosemanticity is 'methodologically out of reach' to establish conclusively.

relationships.condition: Early layers (especially the first ~25% of MLP layers) in 7 LLMs, 70M–6.9B
relationships.reason: Features are represented as sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons (r1). The first 25% of layers show substantially more superposition, inferred from weight statistics and toy-model insights (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Features were represented as sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons, and the first 25% of layers showed substantially more superposition, inferred from weight statistics and toy-model insights.

relationships.condition: Higher-level contextual and linguistic features (e.g. is_python_code), middle layers
relationships.reason: These features appear encoded by seemingly dedicated single neurons rather than spread across many (r3). The authors call this conclusion methodologically inconclusive.
relationships.display_finding: These features appeared to be encoded by seemingly dedicated single neurons rather than spread across many, though the authors call this conclusion methodologically inconclusive.
